clinicalPearls: Inappropriate adduction of the vocal folds during inspiration causes episodic breathlessness and stridor that mimic asthma
Symptoms characteristically feature difficulty getting air in, throat tightness and inspiratory noise localised to the neck
Attacks are often sudden in onset and offset and may be triggered by exercise, irritants, strong smells or stress
It is frequently misdiagnosed as refractory asthma, leading to escalating and ineffective inhaled therapy
Direct laryngoscopy during an episode, showing paradoxical adduction, is the diagnostic gold standard
Speech and language therapy with breathing retraining is the cornerstone of management
reference.pathophysiology: Vocal cord dysfunction, also termed inducible laryngeal obstruction, involves paradoxical closure of the vocal folds during inspiration, transiently narrowing the glottic airway. Laryngeal hyperresponsiveness to triggers such as reflux, postnasal drip, exercise, airborne irritants and psychological stress is thought to drive the abnormal reflex adduction. Because the obstruction is at the larynx rather than the lower airways, it produces predominantly inspiratory symptoms and does not respond to bronchodilators, distinguishing it from asthma even though the two can coexist.
additionalInvestigations: Flexible laryngoscopy, ideally during symptoms or after provocation
Spirometry with attention to truncation of the inspiratory flow-volume loop
Assessment for reflux, rhinosinusitis and asthma as triggers or comorbidities
Exercise or irritant challenge where episodes are provoked
redFlags: Stridor with hypoxia or signs of significant airway compromise
Features suggesting a fixed structural airway lesion
reference.prognosis: The condition is not life-threatening in most cases and responds well to breathing retraining and treatment of triggers, though it can be recurrent and disabling if unrecognised.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as refractory asthma and escalating inhaled or oral steroids
Failing to capture the larynx during an episode
Overlooking coexisting asthma, reflux or rhinosinusitis
Not involving speech and language therapy early
